fixes.explanation: True. The text says some believers “…from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, ‘The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.’” (Acts 15:5) They say it out loud, in front of everybody. Now the council has a real question on its table.

Tarsus doesn't show up in this part of the story, friend. Paul and Barnabas are appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem (Acts 15:2). Jerusalem is where the apostles and elders are, so that's where this question is headed.

Joy, and a lot of it. As Paul and Barnabas pass through Phoenicia and Samaria, they recount the conversion of the Gentiles, bringing “…great joy to all the brothers.” (Acts 15:3) That's the news they carried, and joy is what it brought. I think those brothers were smiling long after the visitors left.

It's true, friend. The text says the ones who stood up were believers “…from the party of the Pharisees…” (Acts 15:5) They declared that the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses. True was the pick this time, and I'm still proud of you.

Sacrifice isn't the word Peter uses, friend. He says God “…made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.” (Acts 15:9) Cleansed hearts, and the way is faith. Sacrifice is a big word in the Bible, so I get why it caught your eye.

False is right. Peter calls it “…a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10) He says it about himself and the other Jewish believers, and about their fathers too. So they have not been able to bear it.

That's what some believers from the party of the Pharisees were pushing, but it's not Peter's answer. He says, “…we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” (Acts 15:11) Saved through grace, and the same for both groups. That's his last word on it.

Rome doesn't come up here, friend. The assembly listens as Barnabas and Paul describe “…the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” (Acts 15:12) That's what the text says they're describing, things that already happened. Travel plans aren't what the verse names.

That's right. James, the one who speaks after Barnabas and Paul finish, says, “The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written…” (Acts 15:15) He doesn't only lean on what Peter said. He brings in what is written. Now there's testimony and Scripture on the same page.

The word only doesn't fit here, friend. The quote says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 17:15 would be the wrong place to look, so stay with Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are named in the words themselves, right next to the remnant of men.

David's fallen tent is what gets rebuilt, but the quote doesn't stop with David's house. It says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are named right in the words. That's a bigger list than only the house of David.

False is right. James says, “…we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God.” (Acts 15:19) He doesn't ask for the whole law of Moses. He says not to cause trouble for the ones turning to God. That's his judgment, friend, and the story keeps going from there.

That's the one. James says to abstain “…from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) Compare that to the law of Moses that some believers from the party of the Pharisees wanted the Gentiles to obey (Acts 15:5), and it's a short list. Sexual immorality is right there on it.

Interest isn't on James's list, friend. He says to abstain “…from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) Those are the four things, and charging interest isn't one of them. Sexual immorality is on the list.

False is right. The letter says, “…some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.” (Acts 15:24) So the leaders say those men went out without their authorization. They weren't sent by the apostles and elders.

Yes. The letter says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) So the message comes two ways, on paper and by voice. That's some good backup, friend.

Appointing elders isn't what the letter says. It says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) Their job is to tell it in person. The same things the letter says, spoken out loud.

That's right. The letter says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements…” (Acts 15:28) The Holy Spirit is named first in that sentence. The apostles and elders stand right beside Him as the ones it seemed good to.
It's true, friend. The text says, “When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message.” (Acts 15:31) Rejoiced is the word the text gives, and the message is called encouraging.

Priests is a reasonable guess with so much law talk in the air, friend, but it's not the word the text uses. It says Judas and Silas, “…who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.” (Acts 15:32) They're called prophets, and what they did was encourage and strengthen the brothers.
